questions.q: How is a single-qubit gate physically implemented on a trapped-ion processor?
options: A precisely tuned laser pulse (or a Raman transition using a pair of lasers) is aimed at one ion for a controlled duration, driving a transition between its two qubit states
A microwave pulse is sent through a dedicated wire connected directly to the ion
The ion is physically rotated inside the trap using the electrode voltages
A magnetic field is pulsed across the entire vacuum chamber, affecting every ion identically
questions.explain: Trapped-ion single-qubit gates are driven optically -- a laser pulse (often via a Raman transition) targets one ion and its duration/intensity set the rotation -- unlike superconducting qubits, which use microwave pulses through dedicated wiring.

questions.q: What physical mechanism allows a two-qubit gate to entangle two ions that are not in direct contact?
options: Laser pulses briefly and reversibly couple each ion's qubit state to a shared vibrational (motional) mode of the whole chain, letting that shared motion carry entanglement between them
The two ions are moved until they physically touch each other
A wire is run between the two ions' positions in the trap
Two-qubit gates are not possible on trapped-ion hardware; only single-qubit gates are
questions.explain: Because ions in a chain share collective motional modes (phonons) through their Coulomb coupling, laser pulses can use that shared motion as a bus to entangle two ions without any direct physical connection between them.

options: The standard trapped-ion two-qubit gate, which uses laser beams detuned from the chain's vibrational frequencies to generate entanglement via a shared motional mode
A gate used exclusively to cool the ion chain before computation begins
A superconducting two-qubit gate implemented with microwave resonators
A method for loading new ions into an empty trap
questions.explain: The MS gate is the widely used trapped-ion two-qubit gate implementation, entangling two selected ions by coupling them through the chain's shared motional (phonon) mode using detuned laser light.

questions.q: Why is laser pointing stability and precision described as the central engineering bottleneck for trapped-ion gate operations?
options: Every gate depends on light landing on the right ion at the right frequency and duration, so small drift in beam pointing, frequency, phase, or intensity translates directly into gate errors
Lasers are only used for taking photographs of the ion chain, not for actual computation
Laser precision only matters for cooling, not for gate operations themselves
Trapped-ion systems don't actually use lasers for gates, only for loading ions into the trap
questions.explain: Because gates rely entirely on optical control, imperfections in beam pointing, frequency lock, phase, or intensity compound into rotation and entanglement errors -- making stabilized optics, not chip fabrication, the dominant engineering challenge.

questions.q: Roughly how do trapped-ion two-qubit gate speeds compare to superconducting two-qubit gate speeds?
options: Trapped-ion gates are generally much slower -- superconducting gates often run in roughly tens of nanoseconds, while ion gates typically take microseconds to a few hundred microseconds, a gap of roughly two to three orders of magnitude
Trapped-ion gates are always faster than superconducting gates, by design
The two platforms have identical gate speeds in all cases
Gate speed has never been measured or compared between the two platforms
questions.explain: Trapped-ion two-qubit gates rely on a comparatively slow mechanical process involving the chain's vibrational motion, making them typically on the order of hundreds of times slower than superconducting gates -- exact figures vary by system and should be treated as illustrative, not fixed.
